To establish an 8(a)(1) violation based on an adverse employment action where the
motive for the action is disputed, the General Counsel has the initial burden of showing that
protected activity was a motivating factor for the action, Wright Line, 251 NLRB 1083 (1980).6
The General Counsel satisfies that burden by proving the existence of protected activity, the25
employer’s knowledge of the activity, and animus against the activity that is sufficient to create 
an inference that the employee’s protected activity was a motivating factor in his or her 
discharge or other discriminatory action. If the General Counsel meets this burden, the burden 
shifts to the employer to demonstrate that the same action would have taken place even in the 
absence of the protected conduct. 730
Tammy Snyder engaged in concerted protected activity by discussing wages with Lisa 
Smallbrock in March 2023 and with Alisa Rowley sometime between March and July 6, 2023.  
Her discussions with Rowley are concerted in that it was a part of a joint effort to obtain a wage 
increase for Rowley.35
Assisting other employees affected by the employer's action or inaction falls within the 
Act's “mutual aid and protection” clause of Section 7, even if the assisting employee is not 
personally affected, American Medical Response of the Mid-Atlantic, 369 NLRB No. 125

spondent violated Section 8(a)(3) and (1) of the Act by re-
fusing to hire Classic’s employees because they were rep-
resented by the Union and in order to avoid an obligation 
to bargain with the Union .  The judge further found that 
the Respondent continued operating the valet parking ser-
vices at Stony Brook in basically unchanged form.  In ad-
dition, the judge found that in light of the unlawful refusal 
to hire the predecessor employees, it must be presume d 
that the Respondent’s workforce would have consisted of 
all or substantially all of Classic’s employees if it had 
hired applicants on a nondiscriminatory basis, as the Re-
spondent’s unlawful hiring practices made it impossible to 
determine otherwise.  The  judge therefore found that un-
der NLRB v. Burns International Security Services, Inc ., 
406 U.S. 272 (1972), the Respondent was a successor to 
Classic, and that it violated Section 8(a)(5) and (1) of the 
Act by refusing to recognize and bargain with the Union.  
Citing Love’s Barbeque Restaurant No. 62 , 245 NLRB 78, 
82 (1979), enfd. in part sub nom. Kallmann v. NLRB , 640 
F.2d 1094 (9th Cir. 1981), the judge additionally found 
that, having unlawfully refused to hire all or substantiall y 
all of the predecessor’ s employees in order to evade suc-
cessorship, the Respondent further violated Section 
8(a)(5) and (1) by unilaterally imposing initial employ-
ment terms that differed from those of the predecessor.  
The judge’s recommended Order therefore required the 
Respondent to offer instatement to the former Classic em-
ployees, to make them whole, and to restore Classic’s  
terms and conditions of employment until the parties ne-
gotiate to agreement or impasse. 4
